hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when someone praises you or blames you, how long does it stay with you?
options: Praise, a minute. Blame, all week
then today’s word is for you. listen.
then you may like this old monk. listen.

steps.line: A well-known Zen story tells of Hakuin, a teacher in a Japanese village, praised by all his neighbors as a man who lived a pure life.
steps.label: a well-known Zen story

steps.line: Then a young woman nearby found she was expecting a baby. Pressed by her angry parents, she named Hakuin as the father. They stormed to his door.

steps.q: They shout at him. He answers only, “Is that so?” When the baby is born, what do the parents do?
o: Take him before the village court
Bring the baby for him to raise
Move away to hide their shame
steps.why: They handed him the baby. No argument, no complaint: he simply took the child in.

steps.line: Hakuin listened, and said only, “Is that so?” When the baby was born, they brought the child to him. He took the baby in.
His good name was gone, and people turned away. But he cared for the baby tenderly, asking neighbors for the milk it needed.

steps.q: His name is ruined, and this baby isn’t his. Why does he care for it so tenderly?
o: The baby needed him, whatever people said
To prove the rumors wrong someday
He hoped the village would forgive him
steps.why: The old commentator Buddhaghosa warns of a ‘near enemy’ of equanimity: dull indifference that looks calm. Hakuin’s calm stayed warm.

steps.line: A year later, the young mother told the truth: the father was a young man from the fish market. Her parents hurried back to apologize and take the child home.

steps.q: A year later, the parents come back for the baby. What does Hakuin do?
o: Asks to stay in the child’s life
Asks for a day to say goodbye
Hands the child back right away
steps.why: He handed back a child he’d raised for a year, and said only, “Is that so?” No victory lap, no request to fix his name.

steps.line: Hakuin gently handed back the child. All he said was, “Is that so?”

steps.q: The Buddha named eight ‘worldly winds’ in four pairs: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, and one more. Which?
steps.why: Pleasure and pain. The Buddha said all eight blow through every life, wise or not; the difference is whether they knock you over.

steps.pre: The Dhammapada says the wise aren’t moved by blame and praise, just as a solid
steps.why: Rock: in Pali, a single solid block. Dhammapada verse 81. Not a tree that bends; a rock that doesn’t need to.

steps.line: Today, a glowing review and a harsh comment, in the same hour. The winds still blow. The rock still feels them. It just doesn’t move.
steps.label: today

say: upekkha, equanimity, is the fourth divine abode. the word means looking on, from a steady place. not looking away. the buddha named eight worldly winds: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. they come to everyone.

hakuin belongs to zen, the school that grew in china and japan, where teachers often show the teaching in a few plain words. theravada teachers point to the same calm in the buddha’s own discourses. both say it: feel the wind. don’t be blown away.

steps.q: Hakuin said the same three words when he was blamed and when he was cleared. What does that show?
o: He was too proud to argue either way
He’d stopped caring how things turned out
His calm didn’t hang on what people said
steps.why: Blame and praise were both just weather. What he actually did, caring for a child, never changed with it.

today.say: today, when praise or blame comes your way, try hakuin’s three words inside: is that so? then do the next kind thing.
options: is that so? good. let me know.
Blame is too hard for that
it is hard. start with praise. it’s a wind too.

card.keepWhy: Is that so? Then the next kind thing.
sources: “Is That So?”, a story about Hakuin Ekaku (1686–1769) in Nyogen Senzaki and Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1939), reprinted in Zen Flesh, Zen Bones (1957)
Dhammapada 81 (Max Müller 1881): “As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise”
Lokavipatti Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 8.6): the eight worldly conditions
Visuddhimagga IX: the near enemy of equanimity (unknowing indifference)
check: The story comes from the Senzaki and Reps English collection (1939); no older Japanese source is confirmed, so it is framed as “a well-known Zen story.”
